source_read: PDF PDFs/Ketamine/Lahti_1995_KetaminePsychosisSchizophrenia.pdf, printed pp. 9-19 (11 PDF pages; PDF page N is printed page 8+N). Scanned pages with an error-prone text layer, so every number used was checked on pages rendered at 150 dpi: the abstract (p. 9), Methods (pp. 10-12), Results (pp. 12-13), Table 1 (p. 11), Table 2 (p. 13), Table 3 (p. 14), Table 4 and Figure 2 (p. 15), Figure 1 (p. 12).

claims.overstatement: The claim is careful and in several places stricter than the paper; the wording does not overstate the source. Four points for the editor. (1) The part not supported (see note): 'at 90 and 180 minutes every value is at or below its own baseline' is true of the BPRS total in all four conditions but not of the psychosis subscale at 0.1 and 0.3 mg/kg, where 7.0 at both times sits above baselines of 6.8 and 6.6, and Table 2 marks the 0.1 mg/kg value at 180 minutes as significant. The statement's own sentence, 'scores were back at or below their own baseline at 90 and 180 minutes', carries the same difficulty. (2) '9 inpatients ... received ... salt water and three amounts' is true of the design but not of everyone: two of the nine did not receive the largest amount (one for an unrelated infection, two for safety across the whole series) and were given a blinded placebo substitution, which is why Table 2 reads n = 7 there. The magnitude's '(n = 9, 9, 9 and 7)' is right. (3) '(SD 6.0)' is an inference: the paper never says whether the values in parentheses are SD or SEM (the magnitudes make sense only as SD). (4) 'The paper gives their timing three different ways' is if anything generous: the abstract says 8-24 hours, the Results say about 6 to 8 hours, Table 3's column header says 4-24 hr, and its entries say 12 hrs, 2 nights and several days.
claims.note: Every number checked on the rendered pages. Table 2 (p. 13) confirms the BPRS totals 34.6 (7.0), 33.4 (6.0), 32.6 (5.2), 31.1 (4.1) for placebo; 33.2 (4.2), 38.3 (7.1), 30.9 (3.2), 29.6 (4.1) at 0.1; 35.2 (5.4), 39.3 (5.0), 33.4 (4.3), 33.7 (3.8) at 0.3; 36.9 (11.0), 45.3 (7.7), 32.3 (5.6), 32.3 (8.0) at 0.5; and the psychosis subscale 8.1, 8.0, 8.0, 7.9; 6.8, 9.8 (3.3), 7.0, 7.0; 6.6, 9.3 (2.8), 7.0, 7.0; 6.9, 12.3 (2.5), 6.6, 6.7, with n = 9, 9, 9 and 7. The p values (.005, .01 for the total; .05, .02 for the psychosis subscale) are as printed on p. 12, as are 'seven of the nine ... at least a 50% increase', 'one showed a change less than 25% and one patient failed to change', the one-in-50%-worse and one-in-60%-better deficit-syndrome pair, and the four delayed-report cases. Table 4 (p. 15) confirms the off-haloperidol totals 37.3 (7.5) and 46.6 (5.9) with footnote p < .1, the text's p = 0.07, n = 6 and 5, and that no psychosis-score rise carries a mark. Figure 2 (p. 15) confirms that the paired on- against off-haloperidol comparison has n = 4 at the largest amount. The claim's last sentence also checks out: no F, t, confidence interval or effect size is printed anywhere in the paper, only p values.

anchors.locator: Methods › Subjects; Experimental Overview; Ketamine Administration Procedure
anchors.extracted: Nine inpatient volunteers with DSM-III-R schizophrenia (5 men, 4 women; mean age 30, +/- 9.3; mean length of illness 9.3 years, +/- 6.2), actively psychotic but stable on a fixed 0.3 mg/kg/day of haloperidol for 4 weeks before the first ketamine day. Four intravenous injections over 60 seconds each (study conditions: placebo and ketamine 0.1, 0.3 and 0.5 mg/kg), one on each of four days spaced over 2 weeks. Order was selected by non-blind staff for safety, not randomized; 11 different orders were used across the 15 series (9 on haloperidol, 6 off); the largest amount was routinely not given first. Three people did not receive the largest amount across the whole study (two for safety, judged by the non-blind observer with the blind preserved, and one for an unrelated infection); the first two received placebo blindly as a substitution. Recruitment was capped at the minimum number by the ethics board. No comparison group without schizophrenia.

anchors.locator: Methods › Mental Status Evaluation; Data Analysis
anchors.extracted: BPRS and the SANS global items rated at baseline and 20, 90 and 180 minutes after injection, from a clinical interview covering everything since the previous rating, by a single research clinician blind to condition; sessions audiotaped. A follow-up clinical interview, also blind, at 8 and 24 hours. BPRS subscales: psychosis (items 4, 12, 15), withdrawal (3, 13, 16), activation (6, 7, 17), anxiety (1, 2, 5, 9), hostility (10, 11, 14). Analysis: multivariate repeated-measures ANOVA with dose as the repeated factor at each time point, with planned orthogonal contrasts of each dose against placebo; paired t tests for the on- against off-haloperidol baselines. No blinding check is described anywhere.

anchors.locator: Results › Ketamine in Haloperidol-Treated Subjects, 1st paragraph (p. 12); Table 2 (p. 13); Figure 1 (p. 12)
anchors.extracted: BPRS total rose at 20 minutes, significantly at 0.3 mg/kg (p = .005) and 0.5 mg/kg (p = .01); totals (mean, dispersion unlabelled) 33.4 (6.0) placebo, 38.3 (7.1), 39.3 (5.0) and 45.3 (7.7), against baselines of 34.6, 33.2, 35.2 and 36.9; totals at 90 and 180 minutes were at or below each condition's own baseline (0.5 mg/kg 32.3 and 32.3). The psychosis subscale accounted for most of the change: 8.0, 9.8 (3.3), 9.3 and 12.3 (2.5) at 20 minutes, significant at 0.1 mg/kg (p = .05) and 0.5 mg/kg (p = .02), against baselines of 8.1, 6.8, 6.6 and 6.9; at 90 and 180 minutes the psychosis values were 7.0 and 7.0 at both 0.1 and 0.3 mg/kg, slightly above their baselines of 6.8 and 6.6, and Table 2 marks the 0.1 mg/kg value at 180 minutes with its p < .05 footnote although it is below the placebo value of 7.9. Seven of the nine had at least a 50% rise in the psychosis score, one changed by less than 25% and one did not change (the oldest, with the longest illness). n = 9, 9, 9 and 7.

anchors.locator: Results › Ketamine in Haloperidol-Treated Subjects, 2nd-3rd paragraphs; Figure 1 legend
anchors.extracted: At 0.1 mg/kg people reported perceptual distortions, illusions and depersonalization; at 0.3 and 0.5 mg/kg, suspiciousness, delusions, typical visual and auditory hallucinations and thought disorder (looseness of associations, incoherence, flight of ideas). In the first 3 to 5 minutes people typically appeared withdrawn but responsive. Figure 1 plots the psychosis subscale with asterisks for a significant increase from the placebo condition at 20 minutes only.

anchors.locator: Results › Ketamine in Haloperidol-Treated Subjects, 4th-6th paragraphs
anchors.extracted: 'Ketamine failed to alter negative mental symptoms in these patients overall (Table 2)': Table 2 contains the BPRS total and its psychosis, withdrawal and anxiety subscales and no SANS or other negative-symptom measure, although the methods name the SANS global items as the negative-symptom measure. Of the two people with prominent enduring negative symptoms meeting deficit-syndrome criteria, one worsened by 50% and the other improved by 60%, with positive symptoms rising in both. Anxiety did not rise except at 0.3 mg/kg at 180 minutes, and tended to fall over the session.

anchors.locator: Results › Ketamine in Haloperidol-Treated Subjects, 7th paragraph (p. 12) continuing on p. 13
anchors.extracted: At the blind follow-up interviews at 8 and 24 hours, 4 of 9 spontaneously reported their psychotic responses returning later: two had ketamine-induced delusions return about 6 to 8 hours afterwards, smaller than the original change, lasting several hours, not severe and needing no treatment, both free of symptoms by 24 hours; one reported active dreaming the night after; a fourth reported the same visual hallucinations recurring occasionally over the next several days and later declined the second, off-haloperidol series because she found them unpleasant. These data are descriptive, gathered by clinical report and not systematically rated, because no delayed effects had been anticipated.

anchors.locator: Results › Ketamine in Neuroleptic-Free Subjects (p. 13); Table 4 and Figure 2 (p. 15)
anchors.extracted: Six people were retested off haloperidol. BPRS total showed only a trend at 20 minutes at 0.5 mg/kg (p = 0.07; Table 4 marks it p < .1): 37.3 (7.5) on placebo against 46.6 (5.9), n = 6 and 5. No psychosis-score rise was significant at any amount. The withdrawal subscale rose significantly (p < .05) at 180 minutes at 0.5 mg/kg (n = 5). Comparing the same people on and off haloperidol, neither the rise in BPRS total and psychosis score at 20 minutes nor the baseline psychosis score differed significantly between conditions; Figure 2 shows the paired comparison rests on n = 6, 6, 6 and 4 on haloperidol against 6, 6, 6 and 5 off it, so at the largest amount only four paired observations, with baseline psychosis scores visibly higher off haloperidol (about 9.8-10.6) than on it (about 7.3-9.2).

anchors.locator: Abstract (p. 9); Results, 7th paragraph (p. 12); Table 3, column header and entries (p. 14)
anchors.extracted: The later effects are given different durations in different places: the abstract says delayed or prolonged (8-24 hours) effects, the Results say about 6 to 8 hours afterwards, Table 3's column is headed 'Delayed Drug Effects (4-24 hr)', and its entries read 'lasted 12 hrs', 'Nightmares while sleeping (2 nights)' and visual hallucinations over 'several days'.

anchors.locator: Table 4 (p. 15), BPRS Psychosis Subscale, 0.5 mg/kg row at 180 minutes
anchors.extracted: Table 4 prints the psychosis subscale at 0.5 mg/kg, 180 minutes, as 38.2 (4.3), which is the same value as the BPRS total in that cell and is impossible on a three-item subscale whose other values run from 9.8 to 12.4; it is a transcription error that the paper does not flag.

key_findings.correction: All values, p values and the four n's confirmed on Table 2 (p. 13) and p. 12. One correction: the paper never says whether the values in parentheses are SD or SEM, in Table 2, Table 4, Table 1 or the Subjects paragraph, so the card's 'SD' should be marked as the editors' reading (the magnitudes are only plausible as SD: 11.0 as a SEM at n = 7 would give an SD of 29 on the BPRS).
Confirmed on Table 2 and p. 12, including the note: Table 2 marks 9.8 and 12.3 with its p < .05 footnote and leaves 9.3 unmarked, with no p value for it in the text.

Confirmed for the BPRS total in all four conditions (the card is right to limit it to the total: on the psychosis subscale the 0.1 and 0.3 mg/kg values at 90 and 180 minutes are 7.0 against baselines of 6.8 and 6.6, i.e. marginally above). The note about no measurement between 20 and 90 minutes is right.
Counts confirmed on p. 12 and patient 8's age 53 and 24 years of illness in Table 1 (p. 11). The editors' percentages recompute: 9.8/6.8 = 1.44, 9.3/6.6 = 1.41, 12.3/6.9 = 1.78.

Table 2 anxiety rows and the text confirmed. Worth adding that the single marked anxiety value (0.3 mg/kg at 180 minutes, 7.3 against placebo 5.6) is one of the isolated 180-minute marks covered by reporting issue 2.
Confirmed on pp. 12-13, including the paper's statement that the reports were descriptive and not systematically rated.
All Table 4 values and the text confirmed (p. 13, p. 15); the trend carries Table 4's p < .1 footnote and the text's p = 0.07.
Confirmed on p. 13 and the Figure 2 legend and axis labels (p. 15): n = 6, 6, 6 and 4 on haloperidol against 6, 6, 6 and 5 off it.

Confirmed on p. 12, including the note that Table 2 holds no negative-symptom measure. Small qualification: the withdrawal subscale did rise slightly from each condition's own baseline at 20 minutes (8.2 to 8.9, 8.0 to 8.8, 7.3 to 8.6 against placebo 7.1 to 7.6), with none marked significant, so 'no increase in withdrawal symptoms' is better put as no significant change.
All design facts confirmed on pp. 11-12.

reporting_issues.note: Independently found: Table 4 prints 38.2 (4.3) in the psychosis row at 180 minutes, the same as the total-score cell.

Confirmed by counting Table 3 (p. 14): visual hallucinations recorded as an acute effect for participants 1-5, with 6 and 7 delusions or disorganized thought only, 8 'No change' and 9 auditory hallucinations only.

Both marks confirmed on Tables 2 and 4, and the 0.3 mg/kg psychosis cell is unmarked. The 0.1 mg/kg psychosis mark at 180 minutes is doubly odd: the value (7.0) is below the placebo value (7.9), so a footnote meaning a significant increase from placebo cannot apply as Figure 1's legend defines it.
Confirmed, and there are more than three: abstract 8-24 hours (p. 9), Results about 6 to 8 hours (p. 12), Table 3 header 4-24 hr with entries of 12 hrs, 2 nights and several days (p. 14).
Confirmed: the Methods name the SANS global items as the negative-symptom measure (p. 11) and no SANS value appears anywhere.
Confirmed: no F, t, df, confidence interval or effect size anywhere; about ten bare p values and the table footnote marks are the whole of the inferential reporting.
Confirmed on Table 2 (n = 7), Table 4 (n = 5) and the Figure 2 labels (n = 4 on haloperidol at the largest amount).
Confirmed on p. 13 ('the 0.5-mg ketamine dose') and in the case vignettes (p. 14).
Confirmed: Figure 1's y-axis reads BPRS Psychosis Score and runs 6 to 14, matching the psychosis subscale, while the sentence citing it reports the total score.
Confirmed from Tables 2 and 4 (placebo baselines 34.6 on haloperidol against 38.3 off it).

risk_of_bias.note: Overall high agreed, and the domain pattern is right for this study: the order of conditions was chosen by non-blind staff rather than randomized (domain 1), raters were unlikely to stay unaware of a condition that produced visible symptoms with no blinding check reported (domain 3), and the set of significant results in the tables does not match the set discussed in the text with no correction for multiplicity (domain 6). I would add to domain 4 that two of the nine did not receive the largest amount on haloperidol and were given a blinded placebo substitution, so the missingness at the top of the dose range is related to how people responded.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial. The title ('stimulate psychosis in schizophrenia') and the abstract's statement that the results 'failed to indicate that haloperidol blocks ketamine-induced psychosis' both go beyond what is shown: the off-haloperidol series is six people, five at the largest amount, with at most four paired observations in the on-against-off comparison and different starting scores, so its null result is an absence of evidence. The negative-symptom conclusion cites a table with no negative-symptom measure in it.

missed: The two people who did not receive the largest amount on haloperidol were given a blinded placebo as a dose substitution (p. 11). That means the placebo column of Table 2 contains, for two people, an injection given in place of the largest amount, which is worth stating beside n = 9 for placebo and n = 7 for 0.5 mg/kg.

The ethics board capped recruitment at the minimum number needed (p. 10), which is the stated reason for n = 9 and belongs in the sample or power fields: the sample size was set by an ethics constraint, not by a power calculation.

The follow-up interviews at 8 and 24 hours were conducted blind to drug and dose by the same clinician (p. 12). That strengthens the delayed-report observations a little relative to 'descriptive clinical report', and the card's key finding 7 and reporting issue 3 could say so.
